prompt: Lesson 1. A program's four goroutines each compute for 400 ms and share nothing. On a machine with `GOMAXPROCS=1` the run takes about 1.6 s. What changed between that run and one taking 0.4 s on four processors?
hint: One word is about the program, the other about the run.

choices.text: The program's concurrency
choices.why: The program, four independent goroutines, was the same in both runs.

choices.text: Only the parallelism the run was given
choices.why: Right. Concurrency is written; parallelism is how many processors run it at once.

choices.text: The number of goroutines the runtime created
choices.why: The loop started four in both runs.

choices.text: The amount of arithmetic each goroutine did
choices.why: Each did the same half-billion multiplications.

prompt: Lesson 1. A service mostly waits on a network. Moved from four processors to one, which prediction does the course support?
hint: A waiting goroutine needs no processor.

choices.text: It slows down about four times, like CPU-bound work
choices.why: That is the prediction for work that computes.

choices.text: It stops working, since goroutines need a processor each
choices.why: Goroutines share processors; a hundred thousand ran on four in lesson 2.

choices.text: It slows down much less, because waits overlap on one processor
choices.why: Right: four one-second waits took one second with `GOMAXPROCS=1`.

choices.text: Its data races disappear
choices.why: Goroutines interleave on one processor too; a race needs no parallelism.

prompt: Lesson 1. `go run -race` printed `WARNING: DATA RACE` and the program exited with status 66. What did the detector do about the race?
hint: Did the total come out right?

choices.text: Reported it, with both places in the source
choices.why: Right. It reports rather than repairs; the total was still wrong.

choices.text: Serialised the two goroutines so the total was right
choices.why: The run printed a wrong total after the reports.

choices.text: Stopped the program at the first conflicting write
choices.why: The program ran to the end and printed its total.

choices.text: Rewrote `total++` as an atomic operation
choices.why: The detector changes nothing in your code.

prompt: Lesson 1. On a machine with no C compiler, what does `go env CGO_ENABLED` print, and what does `go test -race` then do?
hint: The go command looks for `gcc` itself.

choices.text: `1`; it runs without the detector
choices.why: With no compiler found the default is `0`, and `-race` refuses rather than running without itself.

choices.text: `0`; it refuses: `-race requires cgo`
choices.why: Right. Installing `gcc` turns the default back to `1`.

choices.text: `0`; it downloads a compiler and carries on
choices.why: The go command never fetches a C compiler.

choices.text: An error; Go needs `gcc` for every build
choices.why: Ordinary builds need no C at all.

prompt: Lesson 2. `main` starts a goroutine with `go save(record)` and then returns. What happens to `save`?
hint: What does returning from `main` do to the process?

choices.text: It finishes first, because the runtime waits for every goroutine
choices.why: The runtime waits for none; `early.go` printed its greeting in none of five runs.

choices.text: It moves to another process and continues there
choices.why: Goroutines live inside one process and end with it.

choices.text: It ends with the process, possibly before doing anything
choices.why: Right. `main` has to wait on purpose, with `wg.Wait` or a receive.

choices.text: Its return value is stored for the next run
choices.why: A `go` statement throws return values away.

prompt: Lesson 2. A goroutine's stack started at 2048 bytes in `many.go`. How many megabytes (MiB) of stack would 512,000 such goroutines take at the start?
hint: 2 KiB times 512,000, divided by 1024.

prompt: Lesson 2. A goroutine started with `go` panics while `main` is inside a `defer`-protected function with `recover`. What happens?
hint: A panic does not travel to the goroutine that started this one.

choices.text: `main`'s `recover` catches it and the program carries on
choices.why: A `recover` only stops a panic in its own goroutine.

choices.text: The whole program ends with the panic's trace
choices.why: Right. A panic in any goroutine ends the process unless that goroutine recovers it.

choices.text: Only the panicking goroutine ends; `main` never notices
choices.why: `crash.go` showed the whole process ending, `main` included.

choices.text: The runtime restarts the goroutine
choices.why: Go never restarts a goroutine.

prompt: Lesson 2. Match each scheduler term with its meaning.

pairs.right: one of `GOMAXPROCS` licences to run Go code
an idle P taking half of another P's queue

right_distractors: a goroutine waiting on a channel forever

prompt: Lesson 3. Which goroutine should close a channel?
hint: A send after close panics.

choices.text: Any receiver that has read enough
choices.why: A receiver cannot know no sender is about to send.

choices.text: The sender, once it has sent everything
choices.why: Right, once. With several senders, a goroutine that waits for all of them.

choices.text: The garbage collector, when nobody refers to it
choices.why: The collector frees channels; it never closes them.

choices.text: Whichever goroutine made it with `make`
choices.why: Making a channel says nothing about who sends on it.

prompt: Lesson 3. `v, ok := <-ch` returns `0` and `false`. What does that tell you?
hint: Somebody may also send a genuine 0.

choices.text: Somebody sent 0
choices.why: A sent 0 arrives with `ok` true.

choices.text: The channel is nil
choices.why: A receive on a nil channel blocks forever and returns nothing.

choices.text: The channel is closed and has no values left
choices.why: Right. Values sent before the close come first, with `ok` true.

choices.text: The buffer is empty but the channel is open
choices.why: On an open, empty channel the receive would wait.

prompt: Lesson 3. A parameter of type `___ int` lets a function only send on a channel, and the compiler refuses a receive from it.

prompt: Lesson 4. A send on an unbuffered channel has returned. What does the sender know?

choices.text: That the value sits in the channel for later
choices.why: An unbuffered channel holds nothing.

choices.text: That the receiver has finished processing it
choices.why: It knows the value was taken, not what came of it.

choices.text: Nothing more than with a buffered channel
choices.why: A buffered send that returns only says the value is in the buffer.

choices.text: That a receiver has taken the value
choices.why: Right. That meeting is the rendezvous.

prompt: Lesson 4. Order these channels by how many values a sender can leave in them without anybody receiving, fewest first.
hint: The size after the type is the room.

prompt: Lesson 4. A server goroutine is stuck forever on a send nobody will receive, while other goroutines keep serving. What reports it?
hint: When does the runtime's deadlock check fire?

choices.text: The runtime, with `all goroutines are asleep`
choices.why: That fires only when every goroutine is blocked.

choices.text: `go vet`, before the program runs
choices.why: `go vet` passed even the plain deadlock of `stuck.go`.

choices.text: Nothing by itself: it is a silent leak
choices.why: Right. Lesson 6 is about finding such goroutines.

choices.text: A panic after the send has waited too long
choices.why: A send has no time limit of its own.

prompt: Lesson 4. A producer makes 1,000 items a second, the consumer handles 900, and the buffer holds 5,000. After how many seconds is the buffer full?
hint: The buffer grows by the difference each second.

prompt: Lesson 5. Two cases of a `select` are ready at the same moment. Which runs?
hint: `fair.go` counted it.

choices.text: The one written first
choices.why: Written order gives no priority.

choices.text: One of them, chosen at random
choices.why: Right, uniformly, so a busy channel cannot starve another.

choices.text: Both, one after the other
choices.why: A `select` runs exactly one case.

choices.text: Neither: the `select` reports a conflict
choices.why: Several ready cases are the ordinary situation.

prompt: Lesson 5. A handler has 300 ms to answer and collects partial results from a channel in a loop. Where should the `time.After` go?
hint: One clock for the whole answer, or a fresh one each step?

choices.text: Inside the loop, so each receive gets 300 ms
choices.why: Then a steady trickle of results could keep the handler going for ever.

choices.text: Before the loop, made once
choices.why: Right: one deadline for the whole collection, as the `overall` loop of `budget.go`.

choices.text: In a `default` case
choices.why: A `default` never waits, so it is no timeout at all.

choices.text: Nowhere: a buffered channel makes it unnecessary
choices.why: A buffer does nothing about a source that answers slowly.

prompt: Lesson 5. Why is `for { select { case v := <-ch: …; default: } }` a bad way to wait for a value?
hint: Compare the `user` times of `patient` and `restless`.

choices.text: It misses values that arrive while `default` runs
choices.why: A value sent on a channel waits for its receiver; none are missed.

choices.text: It deadlocks when the channel is empty
choices.why: It never blocks at all, which is the problem.

choices.text: It keeps a processor busy the whole time
choices.why: Right: 994 ms of processor in one second, against 3 for a plain receive.

choices.text: `select` refuses a `default` inside a loop
choices.why: It compiles and runs; it just spins.

prompt: A function starts three goroutines that each send a result on an unbuffered channel, receives one result and returns. What happens to the other two goroutines?
hint: Who receives their sends?

choices.text: They are stopped when the function returns
choices.why: Nothing stops a goroutine from outside; returning does not end the goroutines it started.

choices.text: They block on their sends for the rest of the program
choices.why: Right: a leak of two goroutines per call.

choices.text: Their values wait in the channel for the next call
choices.why: An unbuffered channel holds no values; each call also makes a new channel.

choices.text: The program panics with a send on a closed channel
choices.why: Nothing closes the channel; the sends simply wait.

prompt: A service's `goroutineleak` profile reports `total 0`, yet `runtime.NumGoroutine` climbs every hour at rest. What is the most likely explanation?
hint: What does the leak profile have to prove?

choices.text: The goroutine count is wrong
choices.why: The count is exact; the profile is the one that can only report what it proves.

choices.text: The goroutines are running, so they are not a leak
choices.why: A service at rest whose count keeps rising is leaking, whatever they are doing.

choices.text: They wait on something still reachable, such as a channel kept in a global
choices.why: Right: reachability defeats the proof, as in `hidden.go`.

choices.text: The leak profile needs the race detector
choices.why: It needs no race detector; it runs a garbage collection that looks for stuck goroutines.

prompt: Which changes stop a goroutine that ranges over a channel from leaking when its caller returns early? Choose all that apply.
hint: The range ends when the channel is closed.

choices.text: `defer close(ch)` right after `make`
choices.why: Yes, it runs on every path.

choices.text: A `time.Sleep` before the early `return`
choices.why: Waiting closes nothing.

choices.text: A `close(ch)` before every `return`
choices.why: Yes, though the next `return` somebody adds will need one too.

choices.text: Making the channel buffered
choices.why: A buffer helps a sender; the receiver still waits for a close.

prompt: The function in package `runtime` that reports how many goroutines exist right now is `runtime.___`.
hint: It was on every dashboard in lesson 6.

prompt: In a worker pool, which goroutine should close the results channel?
hint: It has to know that every worker has finished.

choices.text: The last worker to finish
choices.why: No worker knows it is the last.

choices.text: The producer, after sending the last job
choices.why: Workers may still be sending results then.

choices.text: One that waits on the workers' `WaitGroup` first
choices.why: Right: after `wg.Wait`, nothing will send again.

choices.text: The reader, when it has the results it wants
choices.why: Closing from the receiving side makes the workers' next send panic.

prompt: A job mostly waits for a database that accepts 40 connections, 10 of which other services use. The machine has 8 processors. What pool size does lesson 7's reasoning give?
hint: For waiting work, look at the other end.

choices.text: 8, one per processor
choices.why: That is the rule for computing work.

choices.text: About 30
choices.why: Right: the limit on the other end minus its other users.

choices.text: 40, the database's limit
choices.why: Ten of those are already in use elsewhere.

choices.text: As many as there are jobs
choices.why: That is the unbounded program that ran out of files.

prompt: A pool of 20 workers runs 400 jobs of 50 ms each, all waiting, nothing else limiting them. About how many milliseconds should the run take?
hint: How many rounds of twenty?

prompt: In the semaphore pattern, why is the place taken with `sem <- struct{}{}` before the `go` statement rather than inside the goroutine?
hint: What would exist at once otherwise?

choices.text: Inside the goroutine the send would panic
choices.why: It would work; it would just limit less.

choices.text: So the number of goroutines is bounded too, not only the work
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: So the jobs run in the order they were listed
choices.why: Goroutines finish in no promised order either way.

choices.text: Because a buffered channel cannot be used inside a goroutine
choices.why: Channels work in any goroutine.

prompt: Four goroutines increment a shared `int` 100,000 times each with `mu.Lock(); n++; mu.Unlock()`. What does the program print?
hint: The mutex makes the increment one step.

choices.text: A different total below 400,000 each run
choices.why: That was lesson 1's program without the mutex.

choices.text: 400,000 every run
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: 100,000, because only one goroutine gets the lock
choices.why: Each takes it in turn, many times over.

choices.text: Nothing: the goroutines deadlock
choices.why: Every `Lock` is followed by an `Unlock`, so nobody waits forever.

prompt: A struct with a `sync.Mutex` field has a method `func (s Store) Put(k, v string)` that locks and writes to a map field. The program has data races and loses no writes in tests. What is wrong?
hint: What does a value receiver copy, and what does it share?

choices.text: The map should be a `sync.Map`
choices.why: The real fault is the copied lock; the map itself is guarded once the receiver is fixed.

choices.text: Each call locks its own copy of the mutex, while the map inside is shared
choices.why: Right. Copying the struct copies the mutex, but a map value is a reference, so every copy writes to the same map unguarded. A pointer receiver fixes it.

choices.text: `defer` must not be used with `Unlock`
choices.why: `defer mu.Unlock()` is the recommended habit.

choices.text: Methods cannot lock a mutex they did not create
choices.why: Any code holding the mutex may lock it.

prompt: When is an `RWMutex` likely to beat a plain `Mutex`, by lesson 8's measurements?
hint: Compare the `work 200` and `work 0` runs.

choices.text: Many readers that hold the lock long enough to overlap
choices.why: Right: three times faster with work under the lock, slower without.

choices.text: Any time there are more readers than writers
choices.why: With a single lookup under the lock, it was slower.

choices.text: When writers are frequent and long
choices.why: A writer holds an `RWMutex` alone; frequent writers remove its advantage.

choices.text: When a reader must upgrade its lock to write
choices.why: An `RLock` cannot be upgraded; trying waits forever.

prompt: Why must `wg.Add(1)` be called before the `go` statement rather than as the goroutine's first line?

choices.text: `Wait` finds the counter at zero and returns at once

choices.text: The goroutine cannot see the `WaitGroup`

choices.text: It makes `Done` run twice

prompt: A configuration loader uses `sync.OnceValues`. The first call fails because a file is missing; the file is created a second later. What do later calls return?

choices.text: The same error as the first call

choices.text: A panic, because the first call failed

prompt: What does the runtime do when two goroutines write to an ordinary map at the same moment, with no lock?

choices.why: It is a fatal error, beyond `recover`.

choices.text: It stops the program with `fatal error: concurrent map writes` when it detects them

prompt: Lesson 11. A function `func Fetch(id string, ctx context.Context) error` is reviewed. What does the convention ask to change?

choices.text: After 5.2 seconds

choices.text: After about 200 ms, with its parent

choices.text: Until the whole loop has finished
